sourceSpan.excerpt: trivial examples, but the mind body problem is in in essence a philosophical puzzle. It's a conceptual puzzle. Scientists may discover all sorts of facts about minds and brains and what goes on in one being correlated with something going on in the other and so on. But is the mind the brain? or not. What's the connection between the two? There appears to be a philosophical puzzle there because on the one hand, it looks like minds have to be brains or at least physical in order to have any physical effects. On the other hand, it seems they can't possibly be because there seems to be some kind of conceptual obstacle to identifying minds with brains. I won't go into the detail, but there appears to be such a conceptual obstacle. If you are as a scientist want to solve that puzzle and show that minds are brains, you have to do conceptual engineering. You're going to have to employ a philosopher because it's a philosophical conceptual puzzle, not a scientific puzzle. moveEvidence.claimSummary: Scientific correlations between minds and brains do not by themselves resolve the conceptual question whether minds are brains.
moveEvidence.reasonSummary: Physical causal considerations suggest minds must be physical, yet a conceptual obstacle appears to resist identifying mental states with brains.

inferenceSummary.premise: Empirical brain correlations coexist with an unresolved conceptual obstacle to mind-brain identity.
inferenceSummary.inference: Additional empirical findings alone do not remove an obstacle concerning what identification means.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Solving the mind-body problem requires conceptual philosophical work as well as science.
